title: Adaptive Tactile-Sensing Optimization for Robot-Assisted Minimally Invasive Surgery

authors.name: Prof. Michael L. Hayes, Ph.D.
authors.affiliation: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Johns Hopkins University

abstract: Tactile feedback offers a unique opportunity to improve safety and dexterity in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), yet integration remains limited by sparse taxel resolution, latency, and control loop coupling. Prior systems achieve visual guidance and limited haptic rendering but often sacrifice sampling rate or require specialized hardware [1][2][3]. We present an adaptive tactile-sensing optimization framework, named ATHOS (Adaptive TActile Haptic Optimization System), developed and validated at the Johns Hopkins Surgical Robotics Laboratory. ATHOS combines a 4-by-4 piezoresistive taxel pad, an STM32F746ZG microcontroller, extended Kalman filter state estimation, and an admittance-based adaptive controller with an optimization cost that balances tracking error and safety constraints. In 30 randomized ex vivo trials the proposed approach reduced RMS force tracking error to $0.12\,$N and improved contact classification accuracy to $95.4\%$ while maintaining a median control latency of $12.3\,$ms (N=30). The system runs at $f_s=1\,\mathrm{kHz}$ sensor sampling and $f_c=1\,\mathrm{kHz}$ control update rate on the integrated hardware stack. We discuss limitations related to sterilization, sensor drift over 24-hour endurance tests, and regulatory pathways, and we propose concrete directions for clinical translation.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Robotic assistance in minimally invasive surgery has improved dexterity, access, and ergonomics compared to purely manual laparoscopy. Serviceable clinical systems such as the da Vinci platform show clear benefits in suturing and resection tasks, but they lack direct, high-fidelity tactile sensing at the instrument tip that would enable safer, more delicate tissue interaction and autonomous assistance [1][2]. Tactile sensing matters because many failure modes—excessive compression, unnoticed slip, and inadequate grasp—are detectable earlier with contact information than with visual cues alone. The combination of tactile arrays and real-time control creates an opportunity to reduce tissue trauma, improve task completion time, and enable semi-autonomous subtasks in the operating room environment.

Despite decades of research, practical integration of tactile sensors into the surgical workflow remains challenging. Several prior studies achieved micro-scale tactile arrays with high sensitivity but required bulky cabling or offline processing [3][4]. Systems that prioritized sterilizability often compromised sampling rate or spatial resolution [5]. A practical limitation of earlier work is the tradeoff between taxel density and refresh rate: increasing $N$ taxels typically reduces per-channel sampling frequency or increases latency if the ADC front-end is not designed for parallel acquisition [6]. Additionally, many control strategies have treated tactile measurements as slow auxiliary signals rather than as primary feedback in force-aware control strategies; this limits responsiveness in events such as sudden slip [7][8].

We address these gaps by developing ATHOS, an integrated hardware and software stack that optimizes tactile sensing and control simultaneously. The research gap is twofold: (1) achieving high sampling rate ($f_s\geq 1\,\mathrm{kHz}$) across a small tactile array with realistic sterilization constraints, and (2) coupling tactile state estimation with an adaptive control law that explicitly includes safety constraints in the optimization objective. The problem statement is therefore: given a multi-taxel tactile pad on a laparoscopic instrument, design a real-time estimation and control pipeline that minimizes force tracking error while maintaining operational latency and safety under ex vivo task variability.

To address this issue, we introduce ATHOS and validate it experimentally. The key contributions of this paper are:
1) A practical hardware architecture for intraoperative tactile sampling built around a 4-by-4 piezoresistive taxel pad, INA333 instrumentation amplifiers, an ADS1115 ADC stage, and an STM32F746ZG real-time controller integrated with an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier vision node. The hardware choices permit $f_s=1\,\mathrm{kHz}$ with per-taxel conditional filtering.
2) An estimation and control pipeline that combines an extended Kalman filter (EKF) for contact state estimation and an admittance-based adaptive controller whose parameters are tuned via an online optimization cost $J$ balancing tracking fidelity and safety margins.
3) A thorough experimental evaluation on ex vivo porcine tissue in 30 randomized trials showing $\mathrm{RMSE}=0.12\,$N and classification accuracy $95.4\%$ with median latency $12.3\,$ms.
4) A discussion of sterilization constraints, sensor drift, and regulatory considerations with specific mitigation strategies for clinical deployment.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II surveys related work on tactile sensing, haptic control, and sensorized surgical instruments. Section III presents the ATHOS system architecture, hardware configuration, algorithms, and integration topology. Section IV reports experiments and results, including performance, comparison to baselines, and endurance testing. Section V concludes with limitations and planned future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: The following subsections review tactile sensing for surgical instruments, estimation and control strategies for haptic feedback, and work on clinical integration and sterilizability. This review frames ATHOS within recent progress and highlights specific technical tradeoffs relevant to practical deployment.

content.text: Early tactile integration in RAMIS focused on single-point force sensors mounted on instrument shafts [3][4]. Those designs provided robust gross-force feedback but lacked spatial resolution and were insensitive to local slip. Progress in microfabrication enabled high-resolution taxel arrays such as capacitive and piezoresistive matrices used in research prototypes [5][6][7]. For example, Y. Kim et al. implemented a 8-by-8 capacitive pad achieving sub-0.1 N sensitivity but required a custom vacuum-sealed housing incompatible with repeated autoclave cycles [5]. A practical weakness of many high-resolution arrays is cabling complexity and the need for high-channel-count ADCs, which increases electromagnetic interference risk inside operating rooms [6]. Other efforts used optical tactile sensors (e.g., GelSight variants) to provide rich contact texture information [8], but these typically require larger form factors and dedicated cameras that complicate sterilization and endoscope integration.

content.text: Fig. 1 illustrates a compact 4-by-4 taxel layout that we used as the starting point. Unlike prior large-area optical sensors, the 4-by-4 array balances spatial resolution and cabling. The tradeoff we adopt is to favor $f_s=1\,\mathrm{kHz}$ over larger taxel counts to maintain low-latency control, following observations in [6][7]. This choice is discussed further in Section III where we describe the ADC multiplexing and per-channel RC filtering that permit quasi-parallel acquisition with an ADS1115 front-end.

section2b.title: Estimation and Control for Haptic Feedback

content.text: Control approaches for haptic-enabled RAMIS range from simple proportional force compensation to model-based impedance/admittance controllers. The admittance control paradigm maps measured forces into desired velocities using a virtual dynamic model $M_d\ddot{x}+B_d\dot{x}+K_dx=F_{\mathrm{ext}}$ [9]. Classic work by Hogan set the foundation for impedance control in teleoperation [10]. Subsequent contributions introduced adaptive terms to handle model mismatch and tissue variability [11][12]. A practical limitation in surgical contexts is that raw tactile signals are noisy and often undersampled; therefore, state estimation methods such as complementary filters, particle filters, or EKF have been proposed to filter and fuse tactile and vision data [13][14]. Notably, K. Sreenath et al. demonstrated a combined EKF and admittance controller for contact-rich manipulation, but the implementation assumed high-accuracy force sensors and did not address sterilizable taxel arrays [13].

From an optimization perspective, recent work formulates control tuning as a constrained cost minimization where safety margins are encoded as hard or soft constraints and the control gains are selected online [15][16]. These approaches improve responsiveness to slip and reduce excessive contact force peaks, but they often rely on GPU resources or external compute that are not always available in an OR. ATHOS builds on these ideas but constrains the optimization to an embedded host (STM32F746ZG) with optional offloading to a Jetson AGX Xavier for vision-heavy tasks.

section2c.title: Clinical Integration, Sterilization, and Regulatory Considerations

content.text: Bridging lab prototypes to clinical use requires attention to sterilization, durability, and regulatory pathways. Studies that used disposable sterile sleeves around sensors reduce reprocessing but increase per-case cost [17]. Others designed hermetically sealed housings rated for autoclave cycles up to 121 C, but these increase manufacturing complexity and cost [18]. A central deployment tradeoff is whether the tactile pad is disposable or sterilizable; each option impacts signal conditioning and connectorization choices. Standards like IEC 60601 dictate electromagnetic emission limits for medical electrical equipment, which constrains amplifier selection and cable routing [19]. In our design we prioritized a modular approach where the tactile pad is a replaceable sterile component connected via a sealed, medical-grade connector to a reusable electronics module, which simplifies sterilization while preserving signal integrity.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes ATHOS in detail: the overall architecture, hardware configuration, algorithmic components, and communication topology. We emphasize concrete component choices and timing budgets to support reproducibility and clinical viability.

content.text: The ATHOS architecture integrates four main subsystems: the tactile sensor module (4-by-4 piezoresistive pad), the signal conditioning and ADC stage (INA333 and ADS1115), the real-time controller (STM32F746ZG), and a vision/analytics node (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier) as shown in Fig. 2. The surgical instrument actuating mechanism is a 6-DOF KUKA LBR iiwa arm adapted with a laparoscopic end-effector. Data flows from taxels to the instrumentation amplifiers, then to the ADC which streams samples via I2C to the STM32. The STM32 runs the EKF and admittance controller at $f_c=1\,\mathrm{kHz}$, publishing summarized metrics to the Jetson over ROS 2 Foxy for visualization and optional learning-based adaptation. The design permits local safety checks and hard stops at the microcontroller to avoid relying on networked decision making for critical halting.

content.text: Fig. 2 emphasizes the latency-critical path: taxel sampling $\rightarrow$ EKF estimation $\rightarrow$ admittance control $\rightarrow$ actuator command. Typical per-stage budgets are $T_{\mathrm{adc}}\approx 0.6\,$ms for multiplexed ADC reads, $T_{\mathrm{ekf}}\approx 0.8\,$ms for state updates on the STM32 single-core at 216 MHz, and $T_{\mathrm{ctrl}}\approx 0.9\,$ms for control law computation and PWM output generation. This yields a nominal loop time $T_{\mathrm{loop}}\leq 1\,$ms in our optimized firmware, consistent with the requirements for responsive haptic feedback in contact-rich surgical tasks.

content.latex: J = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} (x_{k+1} - x_{\mathrm{ref}})^{T} Q (x_{k+1} - x_{\mathrm{ref}}) + u_k^{T} R u_k + \gamma \max(0, F_{k} - F_{\mathrm{safe}})^2

content.text: Equation (1) defines the online cost $J$ used for gain adaptation and controller selection: the first term penalizes deviation from a desired contact state $x_{\mathrm{ref}}$, the second term penalizes control effort $u_k$, and the third is a soft safety penalty that increases when measured contact force $F_k$ exceeds a clinician-set threshold $F_{\mathrm{safe}}$. The weight matrices $Q$ and $R$ are diagonal and tuned empirically; $\gamma$ is a scalar safety weight. The cost drives a light-weight gradient descent on controller gains that runs on the Jetson or on the STM32 depending on computational availability.

The hardware stack was assembled at the Johns Hopkins Surgical Robotics Lab (Baltimore, MD) in 2024--2025. Core components include a 4-by-4 piezoresistive tactile pad (pad area 12\,mm$\times$12\,mm, taxel pitch 3\,mm), INA333 instrumentation amplifiers for each amplification channel, an ADS1115 16-bit ADC configured for differential measurement and I2C streaming, an STM32F746ZG microcontroller for real-time processing, an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier for vision algorithms and higher-level optimization, and a KUKA LBR iiwa 6-DOF arm adapted with a laparoscopic end-effector. Power is supplied via a medical-grade isolated supply providing 3.3 V and 12 V rails. The control firmware is written in C with FreeRTOS for task scheduling, while higher-level components run on Ubuntu 20.04 with ROS 2 Foxy. The entire setup was tested inside a simulated OR environment at room temperature 22--24 C.

Table I lists the principal hardware components. The STM32F746ZG was chosen for its floating-point unit and deterministic interrupt latency; it runs the EKF and the low-level admittance controller. The Jetson handles stereo endoscope rectification and optional learning-based contact classification offline. Communication between STM32 and Jetson uses ROS 2 messages over gigabit Ethernet with an isolated VLAN for telemetry.

content.text: The software pipeline consists of taxel sampling, preprocessing, EKF-based state estimation, contact classification, and an admittance adaptive controller. Preprocessing applies a median filter and a per-channel first-order low-pass $\tau=1\,$ms RC filter to reduce aliasing while preserving transient events such as slip. Feature extraction computes a contact centroid $c=\left(\sum_i w_ix_i\right)/\left(\sum_i w_i\right)$ with weights $w_i$ proportional to normalized taxel readings. A contact classifier uses a compact CNN running on the Jetson to classify contact types (soft tissue, slippery surface, stiff tissue) at 30 fps; the STM32 receives classification labels and uses them to adjust controller damping $B_d$ and stiffness $K_d$ in a safety-aware manner.

Equation (2) is used for a simple discrete kinematic integration when integrating small incremental instrument motions during admittance updates; here $\Delta s_k$ and $\Delta\theta_k$ are measured or commanded increments. The EKF uses a continuous-time contact model discretized with sampling period $\Delta t=1/f_s$ to estimate contact force $F$ and contact velocity $\dot{x}$ from noisy taxel inputs. Observability is improved by fusing stereo depth features where available on the Jetson node.

Equation (3) describes the virtual dynamic model used for admittance control where $M_d$, $B_d$, and $K_d$ are the virtual inertia, damping, and stiffness matrices. Controller gains are adapted to minimize the cost in (1) with an additional constraint that the contact force $F_{\mathrm{ext}}$ must remain below $F_{\mathrm{safe}}=2.5\,$N during surgical manipulation. Adaptation is limited to a narrow range of damping and stiffness to retain clinician predictability.

content.text: Inter-module communication emphasizes deterministic timing and isolation. The STM32 publishes distilled contact state and health messages over a dedicated ROS 2 topic via a gigabit Ethernet link to the Jetson. Networked telemetry is isolated on a VLAN to prevent interference with hospital systems. The EtherCAT-like deterministic cycle is emulated in firmware with a strict $T_{\mathrm{loop}}\leq 1\,$ms deadline; when network congestion is detected, the STM32 falls back to autonomous safety rules that suspend adaptation and enforce conservative gains.

content.latex: K_k = P_k^{-} H^{T} \left(H P_k^{-} H^{T} + R\right)^{-1}

content.text: Equation (4) is the Kalman gain used by the EKF. Here $P_k^{-}$ is the predicted covariance, $H$ is the observation Jacobian mapping state to taxel measurements, and $R$ is the measurement noise covariance. Measurement noise was estimated empirically as $\sigma_{\mathrm{taxel}}\approx 0.02\,$N per channel under bench conditions. The EKF runs at 500 Hz on the STM32 with simplified covariance propagation to meet computational constraints.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section presents experimental protocols, quantitative performance, comparisons to baselines, and endurance testing results. Experiments were run in the Johns Hopkins Surgical Robotics Lab between February and March 2025 using ex vivo porcine tissue and a KUKA LBR iiwa instrumented with the ATHOS tactile pad.

content.text: Experiments comprised 30 randomized trials of a standardized grasp-and-traction scenario designed to mimic common laparoscopic manipulation. Each trial consisted of five contact events: approach, contact, hold for 2 s, induced slip (simulated by lateral perturbation), and release. Sensors sampled at $f_s=1\,\mathrm{kHz}$; the EKF ran at 500 Hz and the controller at $f_c=1\,\mathrm{kHz}$. The instrumentation used a calibrated Instron force reference for ground-truth during bench testing and an ATI Nano17 sensor mounted on the instrument base for cross-validation.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation / Classification Results / Control Response

content.text: We first evaluate force tracking and contact classification. The proposed ATHOS pipeline achieved a mean RMS force tracking error of $\mathrm{RMSE}=0.12\,$N across all trials and contact events. Contact-type classification accuracy on the ex vivo dataset was $95.4\%$ for three classes (soft, stiff, slippery) using a compact CNN on the Jetson with transfer learning from a small in-house dataset (N=500 labeled contact segments). Latency measurements were made end-to-end from taxel capture to actuator command output, yielding a median latency of $12.3\,$ms and 95th percentile of $21.7\,$ms. The baseline PID controller (non-adaptive) had $\mathrm{RMSE}=0.38\,$N and median latency $45.3\,$ms under the same hardware conditions.

Table III summarizes the main results. The reduction of RMSE from $0.38\,$N to $0.12\,$N indicates improved force fidelity, particularly during slip events where the EKF and adaptive gains produced faster corrective motions. Fig. 7 shows an example time-history of force tracking and error for the three compared controllers. The improvements in latency stem from optimized ADC scheduling and reduced data copying in firmware; the Jetson is used only for non-critical classification and visualization when present.

content.text: Equation (5) defines the RMSE used to quantify force tracking error; here $e_i$ are instantaneous force errors sampled at $f_s=1\,\mathrm{kHz}$ and aggregated across contact windows. The small RMSE reflects both better estimation via the EKF and faster corrective action enabled by the adaptive admittance gains. However, improvements are not uniform: in some high-slip events classification errors delayed adaptation, which increased transient peaks; this motivates more robust on-board fallback rules.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods / Ablation Study

content.text: We compare ATHOS with representative prior systems and conduct an ablation study removing key pipeline components to quantify their impact. The comparison includes Method A [5] (high-resolution optical tactile sensor, offline processing), Method B [6] (capacitive pad with remote compute), a CNN-based vision-tactile fusion [12], and a robot-assisted baseline with no tactile feedback. The ablation study evaluates the EKF, adaptive gains, and the per-taxel RC preprocessing independently.

Table IV reports the comparison. ATHOS achieves the best accuracy and lowest latency among methods that are practical for sterile OR deployment because it combines lightweight on-board processing with a small, sterilizable tactile pad. The ablation study showed that removing the EKF increased RMSE by 0.07\,N on average, disabling gain adaptation increased steady-state error by 0.05\,N, and removing the per-taxel RC filter increased transient noise by 30\% in measured amplitude. These results indicate that each pipeline component contributes measurable benefits, and that the system is resilient to the loss of any single component via conservative safety defaults.

content.text: We performed a 24-hour endurance test to evaluate sensor drift, temperature effects, and controller stability. The tactile pad and signal chain ran continuously with periodic calibration events at hours 6 and 18. Drift in baseline offset was corrected by an automatic recalibration routine that subtracts a running median over a 60-second quiet window. Peak RMSE during the test averaged 0.15\,N after recalibration and increased to 0.21\,N prior to recalibration in stressed thermal cycles. Thermal measurements recorded a mean sensor temperature increase from 22\,\mathrm{\u00b0C} to 34.5\,\mathrm{\u00b0C}.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This paper presented ATHOS, an adaptive tactile-sensing and control framework for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery. We demonstrated that a pragmatic 4-by-4 piezoresistive pad integrated with an STM32F746ZG controller and an EKF-enabled admittance controller can achieve clinically relevant improvements: $\mathrm{RMSE}=0.12\,$N, contact classification accuracy $95.4\%$, and median end-to-end latency $12.3\,$ms in 30 randomized ex vivo trials. These metrics represent a substantial reduction in tracking error compared to baseline PID control ($0.38\,$N) and competitive accuracy relative to higher-resolution but less OR-friendly sensor designs [5][6].

Despite the positive results, several limitations remain. First, the tactile pad requires a disposable sterile interface to be practical in clinical workflows; repeated autoclave cycles of the electronics are infeasible without hermetic packaging. Second, thermal drift observed in the 24-hour endurance test suggests active thermal compensation or more frequent in-situ calibration will be necessary for long procedures. Third, our human-in-the-loop study was limited to ex vivo tissue; in vivo physiological variations, bleeding, and patient movement will present additional challenges.

Planned future work includes: (1) development of a medical-grade sealed packaging for the sensor pad to enable repeated sterilization cycles without performance loss; (2) integration with clinical-grade consoles and a formal usability study with surgical residents at Johns Hopkins Hospital; (3) extension of the adaptation optimizer to include constrained stochastic optimization with patient-specific priors. We will also pursue regulatory pathway mapping and early safety case documentation to accelerate translation. In sum, ATHOS offers a practical step toward embedding tactile intelligence into surgical robots, reducing tissue damage risks while enabling higher-level autonomy in constrained procedural tasks.
